speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) how much additional property taxes does the Government expect to collect in 2024 following the decision to increase property taxes as announced by the Ministry on 30 November 2023; and (b) how much property tax does the Government expect to collect in 2025 after accounting for the one-off rebate in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Property tax payable is based on the annual value (AV) of the property, which is the estimated annual rent of the property.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have seen from past data that AV rises and falls based on market trends.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how property AVs are assessed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) takes reference from rental transactions for similar properties over the course of the year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS also takes into account the property’s attributes such as its location, age, land and floor area, improvement works last done and whether there are specific features like swimming pools.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These moves were intended to enhance the progressivity of our wealth taxes, which I recall Members from both sides of the House had supported during the 2022 Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Lim also asked if the property taxes on owner-occupied properties can be mitigated.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One, property tax rates on owner-occupied properties are lower than non-owner-occupied properties.
On Ms Joan Pereira's question about future property tax rebates, we are prepared to consider if such rebates are needed when we review AVs and property tax payable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the expected property tax collection, in Budget 2022, the Finance Minister announced that the two-step increase in the property tax would raise the property tax revenue by $380 million per year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Minister said that the collection expected is $600 million.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question I have pertains to some feedback that has been received, since people received the absolute dollar amount increase they are expected to pay this year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One, which is quite common, has been a request, other than the rebate, to consider whether a differential rate for property tax can be considered, specifically for those with multiple properties as opposed to those with a single property?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This feedback tends to come from those who are retired and senior.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it is a query to the Minister, whether the Government would consider such a differentiated regime, other than the solution which it has, to moderate or mitigate the rise in property tax, which is the one of rebate?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, the 2024 residential property tax revenue is higher than what we had originally anticipated when we debated this issue in Budget 2022.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The higher-than-expected property tax collection was largely due to higher AVs, that arose as a result of the higher market rentals for residential properties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And to cushion this impact, what we have done, is to provide rebates for owner-occupied properties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The rebate is done for both 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The rebate is on a scale, depending on the property type.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For this year, the rebate is up to 100% but capped at $1,000.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, for HDB 1- and 2-room flats, for example, it is 100%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For 3-room flats, it is 70%; 4-room flats, 50%; 5-room flats, 40%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you go all the way to the private properties, it is 15%, capped at $1,000.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With these rebates, as I have shared earlier in my main reply, the increase in the property tax for owner-occupied properties, including for private properties, would be cushioned.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Of course, there are different ways to do this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are open to exploring whether there are other ways to help seniors and retirees, who are staying in private properties or who may need a bit more time, to pay for their property taxes by instalments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something that we are open to considering.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If I may just share one comment on Mr Singh's question about whether there is a differentiated rate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because if you have multiple properties, you can only claim owner-occupation for one of them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The subsequent properties would be non-owner-occupied, and the rates would then be higher, and you do not get the rebate for those subsequent non-owner-occupied properties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But for the people who are staying on their own and have only one property, that is owner-occupied.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The rates are lower compared to non-owner-occupied properties and we provide them with this property tax rebate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But within my constituency, several of my residents, in fact, 50% of my residents are in private estates and a number of them are retirees.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have no source of income, absolutely no source of income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of them have told me that their increase has gone up by almost 30%.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At the end of the day, the impact on them is absolute, in terms of absolute dollar value.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is high since they do not have any increase in, say, pension or they have got absolutely no income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, what do they do when they face a huge property tax bill that has increased substantially?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I also have residents who are in a similar situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Certainly, I think, we empathise with the situation that the retirees are in because they moved into their houses many years ago.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Now that they are growing older, they enjoy the company of their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They like staying in the neighbourhood, their nice community.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And we understand that for some of them, this increase in the property tax is increasing the amount they need to pay.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, yes, it is an increase, but with the property tax rebate, the increase has been cushioned for a large number of private property owners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There will be some, because of the AV of the properties that they stay in, being on the higher side.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened that the Minister has shared that IRAS is prepared to take into consideration the various circumstances of the owners in the assessment of property tax, such as giving help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there avenues for property owners to challenge the AV assessments, if they do not quite agree with how the AV is assessed, which is based on various factors, such as rental rates, physical attributes and so forth?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Valuation Review Board is an independent tribunal, chaired by a district judge from the State Courts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In my main reply, I mentioned a few factors that they look at – the location, the age and the condition of the property.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But there is also one point that I would like to share with the House, which is that when IRAS reviews the AVs of the residential properties every year, they will look at, generally, what is in the market, and they will exclude outliers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you have one particular property in the neighbourhood, which is an outlier – the rental is particularly high – IRAS would disregard that and it will look at the general market trends in coming up with the assessment for the AVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Just to weigh in on the discussion on the AV applicable to properties where the owners are retirees and there are no income-earning occupiers in these properties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Instead of ad hoc assistance, can IRAS consider having a separate category of owner-occupied property tax rate for properties where they are solely occupied by owners who are retirees?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are retirees who stay with their families.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They own the property; their children and family stay with them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are those who stay on their own, but their children stay nearby, or they stay somewhere else, and they come and visit their parents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, every family would have a different situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Instead of doing that, what we have done is not to provide differentiated rates based on the very varied circumstances that different households would face, but we will provide help through the rebates, which I think is a fair and progressive way.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because, as I mentioned earlier, if you stay in a smaller property, especially HDB flats, you get a higher percentage of the rebate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you stay in a private property, you will still get a rebate, but it is 15% and is capped at $1,000.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It has helped to reduce the property tax payable for many of the households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But, of course, if you stay in a very big house and your AV is very high, then this impact of the property tax rebate may not be as significant because your increase is much higher and it is capped at $1,000.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the large majority of private property owners who stay in the properties like terraces and especially, some of the estates that I think Mr Tan would be familiar with; for this category, for many of them, the property tax rebate has helped to cushion the increase in the property tax payable.
